In an American paper I find this anecdote: "An old lady was being shown the spot on which a hero fell. 'I don't wonder,' she replied. 'It's so slippery I nearly fell there myself.'"

Now that story, which is very old in England, and is familiar here to most adult persons, is usually told of Nelson and the Victory . Indeed it is such a commonplace with facetious visitors to that vessel that the wiser of the guides are at pains to get in with it first. But in America it may be fresh and beginning a new lease of life; it will probably go on forever in all English-speaking countries, on each occasion of its recrudescence finding a few people to whom it is new.

It is a problem why we tend to be so resentful when an editor or a comedian offers us a jest that has done service before. It is, I suppose, in part at any rate, because we have paid our money, either for the paper or the seat, and we experience the sense of having been defrauded. We have been done, we feel, because the bargain, as we understood it, was that we were purchasing novelty. So that when suddenly an old, old jape, which perhaps we have ourselves related—and that of course is an aggravation of the grievance—confronts us, we are indignant. But what, one wonders, would a comic paper or a revue that had nothing old in it be like. We can never know.

message.content:
In an American publication, I encountered this humorous tale: "An old lady was being shown the spot on which a hero fell. 'I don't wonder,' she replied. 'It's so slippery I nearly fell there myself.'"

This anecdote, which has long circulated in England and is well-known among most adults here, typically relates to Nelson and the Victory. It has become such a staple among witty tourists visiting the ship that the more astute guides often make a point to mention it first. However, in the United States, it may still carry a sense of novelty and could be poised for a resurgence, likely to continue to circulate indefinitely among English-speaking audiences, with every revival introducing it to a fresh audience.

There is an interesting dilemma surrounding our reactions when an editor or comedian presents us with a joke that has been previously enjoyed. Part of our irritation stems from the financial investment we've made, whether for a ticket or a subscription, leading us to feel cheated. We perceive ourselves as having been misled, as our expectation was to acquire something original. Thus, when confronted with a timeworn quip, especially one we may have shared ourselves—which only heightens our displeasure—we respond with indignation. Yet, one must ponder: what would a comedic publication or a variety show devoid of any familiar material resemble? This is a question that remains unanswered.
